questions.question: Which of the following is one of the three conditions a noun must meet to take Category 1 i'rāb (ḍamma in raf', fatḥa in naṣb, kasra in jarr)?
options: The noun must be muḍāf to a definite noun
The noun must be a proper noun (ism 'alam)
The noun must be mufrad (singular)
The noun must be masculine (mudhakkar)
questions.explanation: The three conditions are: (1) mufrad (singular), (2) munsarif (accepts tanwīn and kasra), and (3) ṣaḥīḥ in the naḥw sense — its final letter is not a ḥarf 'illah (ا، و، ي).

questions.question: In naḥw, a noun ending in wāw or yā' with sukūn on the preceding letter is given which classification?
options: اسْمٌ مَنْقُوص
جَارٍ مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ
غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِف
اسْمٌ مَقْصُور
questions.explanation: A noun ending in wāw or yā' with sukūn on the preceding letter — such as دَلْوٌ or ظَبْيٌ — is called جَارٍ مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ ('acting like a ṣaḥīḥ noun') and follows Category 1 i'rāb.

questions.question: In مَرَرْتُ بِعُمَرَ, why does عُمَرَ carry a fatḥa rather than kasra?
options: Proper nouns always take fatḥa when preceded by a preposition
عُمَرَ is treated as the object of the verb and therefore in naṣb
The preposition بِ changes the following harakah to fatḥa in formal Arabic
عُمَرَ is ghayr munsarif and cannot take kasra, so fatḥa substitutes for it
questions.explanation: عُمَرَ is ghayr munsarif — it rejects both tanwīn and kasra. When majrūr, fatḥa substitutes for the kasra it cannot take (i'rāb far'ī — secondary i'rāb by substitution of ḥarakāt).

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the four conditions required for أَسْمَاءُ السِّتَّةِ to be declined with wāw, alif, and yā'?
options: The noun must be in the dual (tasniyah) form
The noun must be muḍāf to yā' al-mutakallim
The noun must be singular (muwāḥada), not dual or plural
The noun must be used as the subject (mubtadaʾ) of the sentence
questions.explanation: One of the four conditions is muwāḥada — the noun must be singular. If it is dual or plural, the special wāw/alif/yā' i'rāb does not apply.

questions.question: What single feature distinguishes the dual رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَيْن from the plural رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِين?
options: Whether the noon is sākin or mutaḥarrik
The presence or absence of the noon at the end
The length of the alif in the root
The harakah before the yā' — fatḥa for dual, kasra for plural
questions.explanation: رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَيْن has fatḥa before yā' (tasniyah — 'I saw two Muslims'), while رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِين has kasra before yā' (jam' muzakkar sālim — 'I saw many Muslims'). Confusing the two entirely changes the meaning.

questions.question: When مُسْلِمُون is made muḍāf to يَاءُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ, what is the FIRST morphological step?
options: The wāw converts to yā'
The noon drops
The two yā's merge with shaddah
The ḍamma changes to kasra
questions.explanation: The first step is that the noon drops when made muḍāf, yielding مُسْلِمُو + يَ. Then the wāw converts to yā', the two yā's merge with shaddah, and finally ḍamma changes to kasra, giving مُسْلِمِيَّ.

questions.question: When a غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٌ noun is majrūr, what marker does it carry instead of kasra?
options: fatḥa
ḍamma
tanwīn
sukūn
questions.explanation: A ghayr munsarif noun rejects both tanwīn and kasra; when majrūr, fatḥa substitutes for the kasra it cannot take.

questions.question: A noun described as جَارٍ مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ follows which i'rāb category?
options: Category 6 (for jam' muzakkar sālim)
Category 5 (for ism maqsur)
Category 3 (for ghayr munsarif nouns)
Category 1 (ḍamma in raf', fatḥa in naṣb, kasra in jarr)
questions.explanation: جَارٍ مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ means 'acting like a ṣaḥīḥ noun.' A noun with wāw or yā' and sukūn on the preceding letter qualifies and follows Category 1 i'rāb.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the أَسْمَاءُ السِّتَّةِ?
options: رَجُلٌ (man)
بَيْتٌ (house)
فَمٌ (mouth)
يَدٌ (hand)
questions.explanation: The six nouns are أَبٌ (father), أَخٌ (brother), حَمٌ (father-in-law), فَمٌ (mouth), هَنٌ, and ذُو (possessor of).

questions.question: When a noun is made muḍāf to يَاءُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ, what happens to its i'rāb across all three cases?
options: The noun drops its final letter entirely
The noun takes fatḥa in all three cases
The noun takes a visible kasra in all three cases
The three cases look identical — i'rāb is taqdiree (hidden)
questions.explanation: When muḍāf to yā' al-mutakallim, all three i'rāb states look identical (e.g., جَاءَ أَخِي / رَأَيْتُ أَخِي / مَرَرْتُ بِأَخِي). The i'rāb is understood from context, not visible on the word.

questions.question: In which i'rāb state does اسْمٌ مَنْقُوصٌ carry a visible harakah?
options: Naṣb only
Raf' only
Jarr only
All three states carry visible markers
questions.explanation: اسْمٌ مَنْقُوصٌ (e.g., الْقَاضِي) carries a visible fatḥa only in naṣb (رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ); its raf' and jarr markers are hidden (taqdiree).

questions.question: نُونُ التَّثْنِيَةِ always carries _____, while the noon of jam' muzakkar sālim always carries _____.
options: ḍamma; kasra
kasra; fatḥa
fatḥa; kasra
sukūn; fatḥa
questions.explanation: نُونُ التَّثْنِيَةِ is always maksūr (kasra), while noon al-jam' is always maftūḥ (fatḥa) — this distinction allows you to tell dual from plural in the naṣb/jarr forms.

questions.question: أُولُو / أُولِي (meaning 'possessors of') follows which i'rāb category?
options: Category 2 (ism maqsur)
Category 4 (asmā' al-sitta)
Category 3 (ghayr munsarif)
Category 6 (same as jam' muzakkar sālim — wāw in raf', yā' in naṣb/jarr)
questions.explanation: أُولُو / أُولِي follows Category 6 — the same pattern as jam' muzakkar sālim, using wāw in raf' and yā' in naṣb/jarr. It is inherently plural and has no singular form in this pattern.

questions.question: Which type of i'rāb is described as لَفْظِيٌّ?
options: I'rāb that is hidden/estimated — the word's form does not change across cases
I'rāb that applies only to pronouns
I'rāb that is visible and explicitly pronounced on the word
I'rāb that substitutes one ḥarakah for another (niyāba)
questions.explanation: Lafẓī i'rāb is visible and explicitly pronounced (e.g., the ḍamma on a regular noun in raf'), as opposed to taqdiree i'rāb, where the word's written and spoken form does not change regardless of case.

questions.question: According to Al-Baqarah 2:7, which of the following is one of the three faculties described as sealed?
options: الْعَقْل (the intellect)
اللِّسَان (the tongue)
الأَيْدِي (the hands)
الأَبْصَار (the eyesight)
questions.explanation: The three sealed faculties are the hearts (الْقُلُوب), the hearing (السَّمْع), and the eyesight (الأَبْصَار). The sealing is a spiritual metaphor (majāz), not a physical condition.

questions.question: Why did Allah devote 13 full verses to the Munafiqeen in Surah Al-Baqarah — more than to the Mu'minoon or the Kafireen?
options: Because of the great danger (خَطَر عَظِيم) they posed from within and the great harm (ضَرَر كَبِير) they could inflict
Because the Munafiqeen were more numerous than the Mu'minoon in Madinah
Because the Munafiqeen asked the Prophet ﷺ many questions requiring detailed answers
Because Allah wished to teach the Mu'minoon how to refute Munafiq arguments
questions.explanation: Allah devoted 13 verses to the Munafiqeen because of the great danger and great harm they pose to the Muslim community from within. After these verses, two parables (مَثَلَان) further expose the inner darkness of their souls.

questions.question: According to Ibn Kathir, what is the definition of نِفَاق?
options: إِظْهَارُ الْخَيْرِ وَإِسْرَارُ الشَّرِّ (displaying goodness outwardly and concealing evil inwardly)
إِظْهَارُ الْكُفْرِ وَإِسْرَارُ الإِيمَانِ (displaying disbelief outwardly and concealing faith inwardly)
مُوَافَقَةُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فِي الظَّاهِرِ فَقَطْ (agreeing with the believers outwardly only)
إِخْفَاءُ الإِيمَانِ خَوْفًا مِنَ الْأَعْدَاء (concealing faith out of fear of enemies)
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir defines nifaq as: النِّفَاقُ هُوَ إِظْهَارُ الْخَيْرِ وَإِسْرَارُ الشَّرِّ — displaying goodness outwardly while concealing evil inwardly.

questions.question: In what sense do the Munafiqeen deceive only themselves (وَمَا يَخْدَعُونَ إِلَّا أَنفُسَهُمْ)?
options: The evil consequence (وَبَال) of their deception returns to them alone
They cannot truly deceive Allah, so technically they deceive no one at all
Their deception is never effective against the believers
They are so foolish they eventually contradict themselves in public
questions.explanation: The evil consequence (وَبَال) of their deception returns to them alone — they are the ones harmed most by their own nifaq. They cannot perceive this due to their excessive heedlessness (تَمَادِي غَفْلَتِهِمْ) and the completeness of their foolishness.

questions.question: In أَلَا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ الْمُفْسِدُونَ, what grammatical role does the pronoun هُمْ play?
options: It is ضَمِيرُ الْفَصْل, restricting the predicate exclusively to this subject
It functions as the subject (mubtadaʾ) of an embedded nominal sentence
It emphasizes plurality, indicating there are many Munafiqeen
It is a pronoun substituting for أَنَّهُمْ mentioned earlier in the verse
questions.explanation: هُمْ here is ضَمِيرُ الْفَصْل placed between the mubtadaʾ and khabar — it restricts the predicate exclusively to this subject, meaning 'it is they and none other' who are the corrupters.

questions.question: Why do descriptions of the Munafiqeen appear exclusively in Madani surahs and not in Makki surahs?
options: The Quran deliberately withheld this topic in Makkah to protect early Muslims from their enemies
The Prophet ﷺ was forbidden to speak about the Munafiqeen while in Makkah
Makki surahs address only aqeedah; Madani surahs address exclusively social and political matters
Nifaq as a social phenomenon only arose in Madinah after the Hijrah, when Islam became the dominant political and social force
questions.explanation: In Makkah, opposition was open — nobody pretended to be Muslim. Nifaq as a social phenomenon arose only in Madinah after the Hijrah, when Islam became dominant and some joined outwardly for worldly or political benefit.

questions.question: What does نُورُ الْبَصِيرَة refer to, according to the mufassirūn?
options: The light of inner insight and imān in the heart
The light of knowledge acquired through formal Islamic study
The physical light perceived by the eyes in darkness
The light of Quranic recitation that illuminates the believer's path
questions.explanation: نُورُ الْبَصِيرَة is the light of inner insight and imān. Accumulated sins gradually obscure it; once lost, there is no pathway (مَسْلَك) for imān to enter or for kufr to exit the heart.

questions.question: What is the ultimate consequence of النِّفَاقُ الِاعْتِقَادِيُّ in the next life?
options: A major sin requiring repentance but not eternal damnation
Eternal Hellfire (يُخَلِّدُ صَاحِبَهُ فِي النَّار)
Temporary punishment before eventual entry into Paradise
Reduced rank in Paradise
questions.explanation: Nifaq I'tiqadi concerns the creed itself — the person inwardly disbelieves while outwardly claiming Islam — and its consequence is eternal Hellfire (يُخَلِّدُ صَاحِبَهُ فِي النَّار), the most severe of all forms of nifaq.

questions.question: Imam al-Baydawi describes the Munafiqeen as الْمُزَبْزَبُ — between which two groups are they wavering?
options: Between the Mu'mineen and the Kafireen
Between the leaders and the followers of the hypocrites
Between the scholars ('ulamā') and the common people
Between the Ansar and the Muhajireen
questions.explanation: الْمُزَبْزَبُ means 'confused/wavering' — the Munafiqeen waver between the Mu'mineen and the Kafireen, fully belonging to neither group.

questions.question: What does the word وَبَال mean in the context of the Munafiqeen deceiving only themselves?
options: The evil or bad consequence of one's own action returning upon oneself
The outward sin visible to other believers
The divine punishment specifically reserved for the Day of Judgment
Spiritual blindness that prevents self-awareness
questions.explanation: وَبَال means the evil/bad consequence or result — the harmful outcome of one's own action returning upon oneself. The Munafiqeen's deception harms themselves most.

questions.question: Imam al-Baydawi applies أَخْبَثُ الْكَفَرَة to the Munafiqeen — from which root and what does it mean?
options: From خَبَا — 'the most concealed,' meaning their kufr is the most hidden
From خَبَثَ — 'the most vile/wicked' among all disbelievers
From خَبَر — 'the most informed,' meaning they know the truth and still reject it
From خَبَّ — 'the most deceptive,' meaning they excel at trickery
questions.explanation: أَخْبَثُ is the superlative of خَبِيث (vile/wicked), from the root خَبَثَ. The Munafiqeen are described as أَخْبَثُ الْكَفَرَة — the most vile of all disbelievers.

questions.question: How does رِجْس differ from نَجَاسَة?
options: The two terms are synonymous and fully interchangeable in the Quran
رِجْس refers only to idols; نَجَاسَة refers exclusively to internal spiritual impurity
رِجْس is moral/spiritual filth; نَجَاسَة is physical ritual impurity
رِجْس is physical ritual impurity; نَجَاسَة is spiritual filth
questions.explanation: رِجْس is moral/spiritual filth or abomination (used for nifaq, kufr, and idols — فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الْأَوْثَان). نَجَاسَة is physical ritual impurity affecting wuḍū and ṣalāh.

questions.question: What is the grammatical function of the particle أَلَا called in Arabic?
options: حَرْفُ النَّفْيِ (particle of negation)
الْمُنَبِّه (alerting/warning particle that draws the listener's attention)
حَرْفُ الشَّرْطِ (conditional particle)
حَرْفُ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ (interrogative particle)
questions.explanation: أَلَا is called الْمُنَبِّه — the alerting/warning particle that draws the listener's full attention before an emphatic statement, as in Allah's refutation of the Munafiqeen in Ayah 12.

questions.question: Where is ضَمِيرُ الْفَصْل placed, and what rhetorical effect does it add?
options: After the khabar; it summarizes the meaning for added emphasis
Before the mubtadaʾ; it introduces a new topic for discussion
Before the verb; it strengthens the meaning of the verbal predicate
Between the mubtadaʾ and khabar; it restricts the predicate exclusively to that subject
questions.explanation: ضَمِيرُ الْفَصْل is placed between the mubtadaʾ and khabar — its grammatical effect is restriction, confirming that the predicate belongs exclusively to that subject and to no one else.

questions.question: Who reported the سَبَبُ النُّزُول for Ayahs 8–20 of Surah Al-Baqarah?
options: Anas ibn Mālik (رضي الله عنه)
'Ā'ishah (رضي الله عنها)
Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه)
Jābir ibn 'Abdullāh (رضي الله عنه)
questions.explanation: The occasion of revelation for these verses was reported by Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه). The named leaders of the Munafiqeen are Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and Mu'tab ibn Qushayr.

questions.question: How many of water's three qualities (color, taste, smell) must be altered by a foreign substance before the water becomes impermissible for ṭahāra?
options: Only taste and smell matter — color alone does not affect the ruling
Even one change makes it impermissible
All three must be changed
Two or more must be changed
questions.explanation: If two or more of the three qualities are altered by a foreign substance, the water is no longer permissible for ṭahāra. If only one quality is changed by a permissible additive such as soap or saffron, ṭahāra remains valid.

questions.question: Which of the following requires ghusl?
options: مَذْي (pre-seminal fluid released during foreplay)
مَنِي (seminal fluid discharged with desire/shahwa)
وَادِي (fluid sometimes seen after urination)
Any discharge that becomes visible after urination
questions.explanation: مَنِي discharged with desire (shahwa) necessitates ghusl. مَذْي and وَادِي only break wuḍū — wash the affected area and make wuḍū; no ghusl is required for either.

questions.question: According to the Ḥanafī madhhab, what size threshold distinguishes ma-e-kalīl from ma-e-kathīr?
options: 10 hand-spans × 10 hand-spans in area
Depth alone determines the category, not surface area
5 hand-spans × 5 hand-spans in area
20 hand-spans × 20 hand-spans in area
questions.explanation: Ma-e-kalīl is less than 10 × 10 hand-spans — any najāsa renders the entire body impure. Ma-e-kathīr is 10 × 10 or more with sufficient depth — najāsa does not render it impure unless one of the three qualities is visibly altered.

questions.question: At what exact moment does water become مَاءٌ مُسْتَعْمَل?
options: When it first comes into contact with a limb being washed
When it is poured from the container into the hand
The moment it drips off/leaves the body after use
After the full wuḍū or ghusl is completed
questions.explanation: Water acquires the status of musta'mal the moment it drips off/leaves the body — while still on the skin it remains ṭahūr. This precise point is the operative Ḥanafī ruling.

questions.question: What is the Ḥanafī response to Imam Malik's use of the Bi'r Budha'a hadith for small stagnant bodies of water?
options: The Ḥanafīs accept the hadith but limit it to wells located in Madinah
Bi'r Budha'a had an underground stream continuously replenishing it — it was effectively flowing water, not stagnant
The hadith applies only to wells, not to ponds or rivers
The Bi'r Budha'a hadith is considered weak (ḍa'īf) and inadmissible
questions.explanation: Bi'r Budha'a had an underground stream continuously replenishing it — it was effectively flowing water (mā' jārī). The hadith therefore cannot override the rule for genuinely still, stagnant small bodies of water.

questions.question: What Quranic dalīl supports the Ḥanafī ruling that an animal with no flowing blood dying in water does not render it impure?
options: Surah Al-A'rāf's description of water as the source of all life
Surah Al-An'ām's statement that flowing blood (الدَّمَ مَسْفُوحًا) is najis — animals without it introduce no najāsa
Surah Al-Mā'idah's permission to eat aquatic animals, implying they are not najis
Surah Al-Baqarah's declaration that all animals were created for human benefit
questions.explanation: The dalīl is from Surah Al-An'ām: flowing blood (الدَّمَ مَسْفُوحًا) is declared najis. An animal with no flowing blood to begin with introduces no najāsa when it dies in water.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes مَاءٌ طَهُور?
options: It is pure only when combined with a cleansing agent such as soap
It is impure but can be purified through boiling or filtering
It is pure in itself and capable of purifying others
It is pure in itself but cannot purify others
questions.explanation: طَهُور has two properties: (1) pure in itself and (2) capable of purifying others. Examples include rainwater, river water, well water, seawater, and spring water.

questions.question: Under the operative Ḥanafī fatwa, why is mā' musta'mal classified as طَاهِر but not مُطَهِّر?
options: It contains traces of najāsa from the body that cannot be removed
It is pure in itself but cannot be used to purify others — it may not be used for wuḍū or ghusl
It can only purify one more time before permanently becoming impure
Its color, taste, or smell has been altered by contact with the limbs
questions.explanation: The operative Ḥanafī fatwa (in line with Imam Muhammad) classifies mā' musta'mal as ṭāhir (pure in itself) but incapable of purifying others — it may not be used for wuḍū or ghusl, though it may be used for istiñjā', irrigation, and general purposes.

questions.question: Under the Ḥanafī ruling, مَاءٌ مُسْتَعْمَل may be used for which of the following?
options: Performing ghusl after janābah
Performing wuḍū before ṣalāh
Renewing an existing wuḍū
Irrigation, cooking, and general household use
questions.explanation: Mā' musta'mal is ṭāhir but not muṭahhar — it may not be used for wuḍū or ghusl, but it may be used for istiñjā', irrigation, cooking, and general purposes.

questions.question: Imam Abu Yusuf classifies mā' musta'mal as نَجَاسَةٌ خَفِيفَة — what does this term mean?
options: Impurity caused specifically by animal products
Impurity that only affects the hands and feet
Ritual impurity that requires ghusl to remove
Minor/light impurity, less severe than najasat-e-ghalizah
questions.explanation: نَجَاسَةٌ خَفِيفَة means minor or light impurity, less severe than najasat-e-ghalizah (major impurity). Imam Abu Yusuf's opinion places mā' musta'mal in this lighter category.

questions.question: الشَّيْخَانِ in the Ḥanafī madhhab refers to which two scholars?
options: Imam Abu Hanifa and Imam Abu Yusuf
Imam Abu Hanifa and Imam Muhammad
Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad
Imam Shafi'i and Imam Malik
questions.explanation: الشَّيْخَانِ refers to Imam Abu Hanifa and Imam Abu Yusuf. الصَّاحِبَانِ refers to Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad — with Imam Abu Yusuf as the scholar shared between both terms.

questions.question: Which scholar appears in BOTH الشَّيْخَانِ and الصَّاحِبَانِ?
options: Imam Abu Yusuf
Imam Abu Hanifa
Imam Zufar
Imam Muhammad
questions.explanation: الشَّيْخَانِ = Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Abu Yusuf; الصَّاحِبَانِ = Imam Abu Yusuf + Imam Muhammad. Imam Abu Yusuf is the shared scholar between both terms.

questions.question: What condition must be met for مَاءٌ جَارٍ to remain pure despite najāsa entering it?
options: No trace (athar) of the najāsa — no change in color, taste, or smell — must remain visible
The water source must originate from a spring or mountain
The amount of najāsa must be less than a dirham in weight
The water must be flowing above a minimum measured speed
questions.explanation: Najāsa entering flowing water does not make it impure as long as no trace of the najāsa — no change in color, taste, or smell — remains visible in the water.

questions.question: What is the ruling on using excessive water (إِسْرَاف) in wuḍū?
options: Makrūh (disliked) but not forbidden
Permitted when performing ghusl but not during wuḍū
Ḥarām (impermissible), even when standing beside a river
Mustaḥab (recommended) as it shows reverence for the prayer
questions.explanation: Using excessive water even in wuḍū is isrāf and is impermissible (ḥarām). The Prophet ﷺ was described as making wuḍū conservatively even when standing beside a river.
